title: Similar COVID shock, different recovery
evidence: COVID shocks: -6.85 vs -6.72; recovery gaps: -3.35 vs 2.12 pp.
why_it_is_surprising: Similar initial damage was followed by sharply different medium-term growth paths.
recommended_chart: GDP growth line chart with pre-COVID baseline
interpretation: The two economies recovered at different speeds after comparable 2020 shocks.
alternative_explanation: Sector composition, policy support, reopening timing, and base effects may differ.
limitation: Descriptive comparison does not identify which factor caused the divergence.

title: Strong recovery with a high inflation bill
evidence: Recovery gap 2.12 pp; inflation cost 3.81 pp.
why_it_is_surprising: Above-peer recovery coincides with above-peer inflation pressure.
recommended_chart: Inflation cost vs recovery gap scatter
interpretation: Growth recovery and higher inflation appeared together.
alternative_explanation: Global food and energy shocks may drive inflation independently of domestic recovery.
limitation: Co-movement is not evidence that recovery caused inflation.

title: Debt rose while recovery stayed weak
evidence: Debt cost 13.02 pp of GDP; recovery gap -8.31 pp.
why_it_is_surprising: A large fiscal balance-sheet change did not coincide with an equally strong growth recovery.
recommended_chart: Debt cost vs recovery gap scatter
interpretation: Higher debt and weaker recovery occurred at the same time.
alternative_explanation: Debt definitions, automatic stabilizers, exchange rates, and denominator effects can matter.
limitation: Gross debt is not net debt and is not directly comparable for every institutional setting.

title: Recovery with contained inflation and debt costs
evidence: Recovery gap 0.01; inflation cost 1.62; debt cost -0.25.
why_it_is_surprising: The economy combines relatively strong recovery with two relatively contained costs.
interpretation: The post-COVID macro mix is favorable relative to ASEAN peers on these dimensions.
alternative_explanation: A low debt change may reflect denominator growth, accounting coverage, or pre-existing fiscal space.
limitation: The conclusion is relative to this sample and period, not a universal resilience ranking.

title: ASEAN's clearest statistical outlier
why_it_is_surprising: The standardized value lies at least two standard deviations from the ASEAN mean.
interpretation: The country is unusually different on growth_volatility_post within this sample.
alternative_explanation: A structural country characteristic or measurement convention may explain the outlier.
limitation: With only ten countries, z-scores are sensitive to individual observations.

title: Positive growth, but still below the old baseline
why_it_is_surprising: Headline growth is positive even though the post-COVID average remains below the pre-COVID norm.
interpretation: The economy resumed growth without fully regaining its earlier pace.
alternative_explanation: Pre-COVID growth may itself have been unusually high or unsustainable.
limitation: Period averages hide year-to-year changes and revisions.

title: Growth recovery without equal labor-market improvement
why_it_is_surprising: Output recovery does not automatically imply lower unemployment.
recommended_chart: Recovery gap vs unemployment change scatter
interpretation: GDP and labor-market recovery moved differently.
alternative_explanation: Labor-force participation and informal employment can affect the unemployment rate.
limitation: WEO unemployment coverage is incomplete for several ASEAN economies.

title: Recovery accompanied by a weaker external balance
evidence: Recovery gap -1.06; current-account change -8.38 pp of GDP.
why_it_is_surprising: Stronger activity coincides with a deterioration in the external balance.
recommended_chart: Recovery gap vs current-account change scatter
interpretation: Recovery and a weaker current account appeared together.
alternative_explanation: Stronger investment or temporary commodity-price effects may widen a deficit.
limitation: A current-account deficit is not automatically a vulnerability; financing quality matters.
